reasons: Passage read in units.jsonl with context and in two further witnesses (LL G800011E:#1/8:32; Windisch IT I L4236-L4237): same Longes sentence, so one Irish witness. Forms: bó nom. sg., míl nom. sg. 'animal' (not 'honey', 'soldier', 'louse'); the animals are milked (no-mbligtis) on hearing the singing. Etymology sound: Matasović PCelt. *mīlo- 'animal' < *meh₁lo-, cogn. Gk μῆλον; Gk βοῦς = OIr. bó. (The automatic map gives smeh₁l; lexicon.jsonl meh₁lo- is a different entry 'measurement, time'; no qualification field on any etymon involved.) Greek μῆλα + βοῦς coordinated is a real formula (Il. 18.524, 23.166; Op. 795; fr. 180.9, all verified). But Irish míl has generalized to 'any beast', so the Irish does not pair cattle with small stock: 'every cow and every animal' is an inclusive list any language could form. Co-occurrence of bó and míl in the Celtic layer is rare outside this text (most regex hits are mil 'honey' or the name Míl). Two exact cognates in coordination is notable, but the Irish attestation is single, prose, semantically shifted, so not compelling.

Read in units.jsonl: Expulsion of the Déssi (Meyer, G302006:#1:156) and LU (G301900:#1/#21:93) are the same sentence in two editions of one text, one witness. gonat = 3pl. ipv. of gonaid, negated by ná; boin acc. sg. of bó; the cow is the druid in cow-shape (G301900:#1/#21:84: rricht 'shape', guin 'slaying') in a ritual/magical frame, not an offence formula. AVŚ 1.16.4 (verified via DCS s9) 'if you kill our cow, horse, man' and RV 1.114.10a goghnám / 7.56.17c gohā́ verified. Etymology exact (OIr. gonaid = Ved. han- < *gʷʰen-; bó = gā́m < *gʷōm), no qualification in lexicon. But *gʷʰen- is the ordinary 'kill' verb in both languages, so 'kill the cow' is what either would say anyway (the claim concedes this). The compound leg is weak: Bóguine rests on Cóir Anmann (G503002:#1/1/210:1), an etymologizing name-tract glossing it with guin + bó, not a securely inherited compound; Greek βουφονέω is only sacrificial slaughter. Contexts are not congruent (Irish prohibition about a shape-shifted druid vs Vedic curse on a killer of livestock). The Indo-Iranian *gʷou-gʷʰen- compound is real, but the Irish adds little beyond generic verb+object.

Read in units.jsonl (LU poem on Diarmait): preceding line t#5:18 has gabra, i.e. the poem's horse word is gabor; ech appears only in the interlinear gloss on the name Grip, so the *h₁eḱwo- member is not in the verse. negar is the passive of nigid (rel. after asa, 'from which ... is washed'), read is plausible; etymologies (nigid = nij- = νίζω; uisce/ὕδωρ root) are fine. But the collocation is not congruent: Vedic áśvaḥ + niktáḥ is a Soma simile (RV 8.2.2c, 9.109.10b verified), the Irish is literal water polluted by blood and unfit for the sacrament (t#5:20), and Greek Il. 11.830 washes a wound, no horse. Washing horses in water is everyday practice; only one shared element (the verb) is actually in the text. Coincidence.

Anchor read in units.jsonl (Immram Brain G303028:#1/#1:19): the wave pours from the sea (mmuir) against (fri) the land (tír) in a description of the otherworld island, a spatial contrast, not a merism of totality; the anchor does not show the claimed phrase. Lucretius 1.3 and 1.30 verified (mare/maria with terras). Etymology: muir = mare (*mori-) exact; tír (Matasović *tīros-, s-stem) and terra (*terseh₂) are root-cognate but different formations. The merism itself occurs in the Celtic layer only in Christian/clerical contexts: annals (eter, muir, tír coordinated; verified e.g. G100004 I1011, G100001C U1511), Síaburcharpat (for + muir + tír, verified G301900:#1/#25/t#2:98-99, G301008:#1/#1/t#2:90-91; a Christianized hell-and-Patrick frame), and the Welsh Bruts, which translate Geoffrey's Latin, so the Welsh vor + thir is a direct rendering of terra-marique. 'Sea and land' for 'everywhere' is a natural merism, and calque from Latin terra-marique is the likelier source; no instance is plausibly pre-Latin. Generic/derivative.

Welsh read in units.jsonl (White Book, Peredur, loathly damsel's portrait, L7915-L7934): 'her two hips (glun, lenited clun f. after dwy) were broad (llydan)' then ŷfcỳanic, probably OCR for esgyrnig 'bony'. Etymology: MW clun 'thigh, hip' = Lat. clūnis, Av. sraoni-, Skt śroṇi- (Matasović *klowni- 'thigh' < *ḱlowni-); llydan < *flitano- < *pl̥th₂-no- (Matasović), root-cognate with Av. pərəθu-, Skt pṛthu- but a different formation. Avestan YtWay12.13f verified: pərəϑu with sraōniš in Vayu's body-epithet list (with dərəzi, bərəzi). So both lexemes are root-cognate, in a body-catalogue in both. Against: Welsh is a predicative clause in a grotesque portrait, not a compound epithet; Indo-Iranian uses it for divine might (Av.) or female beauty (Skt), so contexts are not congruent. 'Broad hips' is a natural description of a body; the Welsh is one instance in a 13th-c. romance whose loathly-damsel portrait has a Continental counterpart (Chrétien's Perceval), which I cannot check from the corpus, so derivation from that is not excluded. Irish lesslethan/uchtlethan (Windisch L14372-L14431, verified) use non-cognate nouns and only show the productive Irish X-lethan compound type, adding no support for *ḱlowni-. Only one Welsh co-occurrence of clun and llydan in the layer.
